content.thinking:
I need to avoid restating the given cost figures as though I computed them myself, and shouldn't supply my own number either—better to describe impact qualitatively while keeping the incident window as given, focusing on root cause, executive summary, and assumptions instead.

I should note the assumptions plainly: I'm inferring a link between the traffic rise and autoscaler flapping from correlated metrics, attributing recovery to the pin even though traffic had already plateaued and might have stabilized on its own, treating the ClientDisconnected errors as a symptom rather than the root cause, and assuming there are no gaps in deploy or feature-flag data.

assumptions: The causal link between the traffic step-up and the autoscaler oscillation is inferred from correlated metrics; no autoscaler controller logs or scaling-decision events were examined.
Recovery is attributed to raising the autoscaler floor, but demand had already plateaued before the change, so the service settling on its own cannot be fully excluded.

The ClientDisconnected errors on the account page are treated as a symptom of slow responses (shoppers abandoning) rather than an independent failure; this was not confirmed against client-side or edge telemetry.
The absence of deploys, config changes, and flag changes is taken from the change-event and flag-provider queries over the window searched; sources outside those systems were not checked.

Only the shop's own logs and metrics were reviewed — no dependency or downstream service was inspected directly, so a contributing upstream slowdown was ruled out only by the absence of dependency-specific log entries.
Impact is assumed limited to the account page, as that is the only surface named in the logs read.
input.executive_summary: On the evening of 28 September 2026, the online shop's account pages became slow for a short period late in the hour, between 22:03 and 22:05 UTC. Traffic to the shop had climbed sharply about twenty minutes earlier and stayed high, and the system that automatically adds and removes computing capacity never settled — it repeatedly added capacity and then took it straight back away. Whenever capacity was pulled back, pages slowed and some shoppers gave up and closed the page before it loaded, which showed up as a modest rise in failed requests above the shop's normal background level. Customers who stayed on the page saw slow account pages; checkout and browsing were not reported as separately affected. The automated on-call system picked up the alert, ruled out recent releases and configuration or feature-flag changes, identified the unsettled capacity controller as the most likely cause, and raised the shop's minimum capacity floor so it could no longer drop back down. Response times returned to normal levels and the incident was closed as mitigated. A draft code change has been proposed to address the underlying scaling behaviour.
input.root_cause: A roughly 4.5x step-up in request volume to io-shop starting around 21:46 UTC put the service's autoscaler into an unstable loop: cpu_limit_cores oscillated between 3.0 and 6.0 every one to three minutes, continuing even after demand plateaued at ~5400 req/min. Each time the limit snapped back to 3 cores while actual CPU use was pegged at or above 3, requests queued and latency spiked into the hundreds-to-thousands of milliseconds, tripping the HighLatency alert; no deploy, config, or feature-flag change was involved, and the ClientDisconnected errors on the account page were shoppers abandoning slow responses rather than a separate fault.
